title: The ten-day retreat, metta day
hookLine: the last day's metta and the return to talking

cards: For days, the dining hall has sounded like spoons and footsteps. Then, near the end of the retreat, silence lifts, and the first words come out as whispers, as if talking were a language half forgotten. Someone laughs.
Then the room roars. People who passed each other again and again without a glance find out names, hometowns, what nearly made them leave.
But before anyone says a word, there's one more sit, and it's different from all the others.

teach.b: First, the word. Metta is the Pali word for loving-kindness, or friendliness: a warm wish for the well-being of others, with no strings attached.

teach.h: THE LAST SIT GIVES IT AWAY.
teach.b: Second, why it comes last. In courses taught in the tradition of S. N.
Goenka, the long days of watching breath and body are followed by a session of metta before silence lifts.

As those teachers give it, a mind made calmer and clearer by days of practice has something to share, and metta is the sharing. You've done the work; now give away what it earned. Third, the old text.
In the discourse on loving-kindness, a short teaching in the collection called the Sutta Nipata, the Buddha describes the heart to cultivate.

teach.h: LIKE A MOTHER WITH HER ONLY CHILD.
teach.b: As a mother would protect her only child with her own life, so one should keep a boundless heart toward all beings: above, below, all around, without hatred or ill will.
Standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake, the text says, keep this mindfulness. Fourth, the return to talking. Metta isn't left on the cushion.

teach.h: THE FIRST TEST IS THE DINING HALL.
teach.b: The first test comes minutes later, in a noisy room, with the person who sniffled through every sit, or the one who took your spot.
The practice changes shape: from watching your own mind to wishing others well, out loud and face to face. Some students say the talking feels harder than the silence was.

how: At the end of ten-day retreats in the tradition of S. N. Goenka, students practice metta, loving-kindness toward all beings, before noble silence is lifted and they begin talking with one another again.

o: a retreat that ends with a big feast and speeches
a retreat that ends with a vow never to speak again
a silent retreat that ends with a sit of loving-kindness

p: protects her only child with her life

s: the retreat ends with one more breath-watching sit
in these courses the last practice is metta, wishing well to all beings.
the discourse on loving-kindness compares it to a mother protecting her only child
so one should keep a boundless heart toward all beings.
metta only counts if you feel warm
the wish counts even when the warmth won't come.

games.q: silence has just lifted. across the dining hall is the person who took your spot every morning. what does metta day ask of you?
o: avoid them; you never spoke anyway.
wish them well, and say hello.
finally tell them about the spot.
games.why: metta isn't left on the cushion. the first test comes in a noisy room, with the people you sat beside.

practice: Begin with the breath, letting the mind quiet, then bring to mind someone you love and wish them well with the simple words teachers often give: may you be well, may you be safe, may you be at ease.
Widen it to someone you barely know, then someone difficult, then everyone, in every direction. If the warmth won't come, that's all right; the wish still counts.

wordCard.voice: The ten-day retreat. At its end, a sit of metta, loving-kindness toward all beings, and then silence lifts and the talking begins. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali metta (Sanskrit maitri): loving-kindness, friendliness, a warm wish for others' well-being.

carryVoice: Your line: metta day. The silence ends, and the wishing goes on. Until tomorrow.
